title: Vertex Solutions - Private VPC discovery
summary: Intro discovery focusing on private/VPC deployment. Customer runs regulated B2B SaaS with strict network controls and data residency needs. Main concerns: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, cross-region endpoints, overlapping CIDR, egress controls, audit logging and KMS integration. Agreed next step: send network questionnaire, schedule technical deep-dive and security pack, run PoC network test windows.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-20 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jasmine Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Evan Chen (Redwood), Aisha Khan (Vertex CTO), Ben Ortiz (Head of Infra), Clara Lee (Security), Dan Morgan (DevOps)

[00:00] Jasmine: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm jasmine from redwood inference, i'll kick us off. quick intros?
[00:12] Aisha: hi, i'm aisha, cto at vertex solutions. we run a b2b analytics platform, heavily regulated, and looking at running llm features inside our VPC.
[00:20] Ben: ben here, infra lead, curious about peering vs endpoints and how traffic egress works.
[00:28] Clara: clara here, security - SOC2 in progress, we'll be looking closely at keys, audit logs, and private connectivity.
[00:32] Marco: hi all, marco from redwood, i'll be the technical lead on this, i'll ask some deep questions about network/topology and latency.

[02:10] Jasmine: high level — we support hosted api, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployments. from what you mentioned in the outreach it sounds like private/vpc is the path. is that correct?
[02:20] Aisha: yes, private for sure. data residency and isolation are musts. we can't send payloads over public internet, and need control plane in our cloud or peered network.
[02:33] Jasmine: got it. we typically offer two private patterns—VPC peering/transit and private endpoints (interface endpoints / PrivateLink depending on cloud). both support private traffic only but tradeoffs around cross-account peering and multi-region work differ.

[03:10] Marco: quick network question — are you on a single AWS account or multi-account org?
[03:17] Ben: we have multiple accounts per team, central infra account for shared services. we use a transit gateway for account-to-account routing today.
[03:26] Marco: ok transit gateway is common—means we can either peer into your infra account or expose an interface endpoint in the shared services account. do you have overlapping CIDRs across accounts?
[03:40] Ben: unfortunately yes, some older teams use 10.0/8 ranges and we have overlaps.
[03:46] Marco: that complicates classic peering; peering doesn't allow overlapping prefixes. PrivateLink/interface endpoints are usually easier in that case because they use ENIs and don't require unique CIDR.

[04:20] Clara: question — how do we handle DNS? we need split-horizon so internal service names resolve to private endpoints and nothing leaks public.
[04:29] Marco: we support private DNS options; on aws we can register private hosted zones and configure split-horizon resolution. for peering we typically update route tables and use conditional forwarding if needed. some transcription notes: our docs say "private-dns" but sometimes product docs call it "split dns" — small mismatch.

[06:00] Dan: latency is a concern. our users need sub-200ms inference for the critical path. if we run private in the same region as our app VPC what does lat look like?
[06:10] Marco: in-region private deployments typically give best latency. hosted API with private egress over a peered connection could add 10-30ms depending on topology; dedicated on same AZs will be lower. we will need to benchmark with your traffic.

[07:05] Aisha: region constraints — we have data residency requirements for EU customers so any model training or inference must not leave eu-west-1. do you have private deployments in eu-west-1?
[07:16] Marco: yes, we support private deployments in several regions including eu-west-1. for strict residency we can run the control plane in your VPC or a customer-managed control plane depending on the package.
[07:35] Jasmine: to add, our private offering can be deployed as a fully customer-managed control plane (on-prem/VPC) or as a redwood-managed control plane but peered into your network; both options have different levels of access.

[08:20] Clara: KMS — can we bring our own keys? keys must stay in our KMS, we can't hand keys to a third party.
[08:28] Marco: yes BYOK is supported. for private deployments we can integrate with your KMS (customer-managed keys), and logs show key usage. for hosted api we can also support customer-managed CMKs in most cases. there are some operational caveats around rotation and service accounts but we document those.

[09:40] Ben: what about egress filtering and NAT? our environment blocks internet egress except through controlled proxies. how does the runtime fetch model artifacts or updates?
[09:52] Marco: good question. for customer-managed deployments, model artifacts can be pre-staged in an S3 bucket within your VPC or via a controlled S3 endpoint. if you prefer no internet egress we support pulling from internal artifact repos via VPC endpoints. for redwood-managed deployments we can push artifacts over a peered link, but we'd need permission and a secure channel.

[11:10] Aisha: do you support transit gateway attachments across regions for multi-region failover?
[11:17] Marco: transit gateway supports inter-region peering in aws, and we can work with that. but cross-region traffic will add latency—if you need strict latency SLOs you'd want region-local serving with data pinned to region. we can also replicate models per-region.

[12:05] Dan: any constraints on port rules or security groups? our security team will want egress locked to specific ranges and ports.
[12:12] Marco: runtime requires outbound HTTPS for control plane interactions if redwood-managed, and gRPC/HTTPS on specific ports internally for tokens and health. we publish a minimal set of egress endpoints and ports. for private, we can restrict to ENI-level security groups and provide exact IP ranges or VPC endpoint ARNs.

[13:40] Clara: audit logs — we need request-level audit trail for compliance and retention for 365 days. do you capture per-request logs?
[13:50] Evan: we run request-level audit logs in Private deployments; logs can be shipped to your logging stack (CloudWatch/ELK/Splunk) over private routes and we can support a retention policy. some metadata like token hashes are stored only in ephemeral caches; we avoid storing raw prompt text in external indexes unless configured.

[15:05] Aisha: ok thanks. let's talk about auth — SSO and RBAC integrations.
[15:12] Marco: we integrate with SAML/Okta for single sign-on to the console, and we support fine-grained RBAC for roles. API keys can be restricted by IP and rotated. for private deployments you can enforce access via your identity provider and the control plane can be configured to use your IdP.

[16:30] Ben: back to network — if we go interface endpoints, what's the traffic path? do we need route table changes?
[16:38] Marco: interface endpoints create ENIs in your subnets; traffic stays within aws fabric and doesn't require peering. DNS maps service names to ENI IPs. Route tables generally don't need changes, but you may need to ensure subnets have room for ENIs and security groups allow the connection.

[17:50] Dan: how do we handle rate limiting and throttles at the edge? we have bursty traffic.
[17:56] Marco: we offer per-route throttles and token quotas. For private deployments we recommend dedicated capacity for predictable throughput; with autoscaling policies you can handle bursts. we can also configure per-customer rate limits at the gateway level in your VPC.
transcript_continued:
[19:30] Clara: any concerns with certificate management for interface endpoints?
[19:36] Marco: we support mutual TLS between services if you want mTLS; otherwise standard TLS with our certs is used. certificates can be provisioned via ACM or customer-supplied certs depending on deployment model.

[20:45] Aisha: are there any gotchas with peering? we've seen issues with route table propagation and blackholing when peering across complex orgs.
[20:55] Marco: yes peering requires careful route management and no overlapping CIDRs. That's why for complex org networks we often recommend PrivateLink; it reduces route table complexity and avoids transitive routing pitfalls. for transit gateways we coordinate with central infra to provision attachments and propagate routes.

[22:10] Ben: about multi-region model replication — how do you keep model versions consistent?
[22:16] Evan: we run a model catalog with version tags and artifacts; replication can be scheduled and we can do checksum verification. for critical models we do canary rollouts region-by-region with automatic fallback to older versions if regressions are detected.

[23:50] Dan: for the pilot we'd like to test with a small traffic slice, maybe 5% of requests routed to redwood private env. is traffic splitting supported?
[23:58] Marco: yes, we support routing policies and can do traffic splits at the API gateway or using DNS-based approaches. For private we can configure canary rules in your gateway to send a portion of traffic to the redwood endpoints.

[25:02] Aisha: security pack — please include encryption in transit at rest details, SOC2 artifact list, pen-test reports, and architecture for BYOK.
[25:12] Jasmine: will do. we'll attach the redwood private security pack and our SOC2 summary.

[26:40] Clara: how about maintenance windows and patching? we need scheduled windows with advance notice.
[26:47] Marco: for customer-managed deployments you control patch windows. for redwood-managed private we provide a maintenance calendar and can set blackout periods. SLA credits for downtime are part of the dedicated/reserved contracts.

[28:10] Ben: any special networking for GPUs? we plan to use g4/g5 nodes in our accounts for other workloads, can we co-locate?
[28:18] Marco: you can co-locate the workload but we'd recommend isolating inference nodes for performance. our runtime benefits from high throughput NICs and placement groups for low latency. we can provide recommended instance types and placement guidance.
transcript_final:
[30:00] Jasmine: recap — action items and next steps: we'll send questionnaire and security pack; schedule the deep-dive; ben to send vpc diagram. any other concerns?
[30:15] Aisha: timing — we'd like PoC in 4-6 weeks if everything checks out.
[30:22] Jasmine: sounds reasonable. Marco will follow up on pilot architecture.
[30:30] Marco: i will also include a short checklist for DNS and route table requirements to avoid the common gotchas.
[30:40] Dan: thanks, one last thing — can you show sample terraform modules or cloudformation for the endpoints?
[30:46] Marco: yes we have terraform examples, i'll include them in the follow-up.

[31:10] Clara: ok thanks everyone.
[31:15] Jasmine: thanks all, we'll follow up by tuesday.

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels may be approximated, occasional transcription errors (e.g., "private link" vs "privatelink"), and minor filler words present.

End of meeting.
